query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Refining the melt-spinning process under a high-purity inert atmosphere with a minimum cooling rate of 1×10^5 K/s, thereby minimizing oxygen ingress and achieving rapid undercooling during solidification, will improve the glass-forming ability and enhance the thermal stability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys relative to otherwise comparable baseline conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys prepared by conventional arc melting.
generation.intervention: Implement a refined melt-spinning strategy under high-purity inert conditions with a measured cooling rate ≥1×10^5 K/s.
generation.conditions: Effective when an adequately low oxygen partial pressure is maintained and when quenching rates reach or exceed 1×10^5 K/s. Less likely to be effective if oxygen levels rise due to insufficient inert-gas purity or if cooling rates are lower than the threshold.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced heterogeneous nucleation due to minimized oxygen contamination during high-rate solidification.
generation.mechanism: High-purity, rapid cooling suppresses the formation of crystallization nuclei, thereby preserving a supercooled liquid region that promotes amorphous-phase formation and delays devitrification.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase of at least 20% in the maximum achievable amorphous sample thickness and a higher onset temperature for crystallization, compared to standard melt-spinning conditions with lower cooling rates and less inert atmosphere control.
generation.baseline: Standard melt-spinning with lower inert-gas purity and cooling rates (~10^4 K/s), producing partial amorphization and lower thermal stability.
generation.boundary: Insufficient inert-gas purity or sub-threshold cooling rates nullify the effect, permitting crystallization and reducing thermal stability gains.
generation.uncertainty: Exact degrees of improvement may vary by alloy composition; further investigations are required to optimize parameters for a particular alloy system.

falsification_experiment.design: Melt-spin the same phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy composition under two conditions: (1) The refined high-purity inert atmosphere with ≥1×10^5 K/s cooling rate, and (2) A standard inert atmosphere at ~10^4 K/s cooling rate. Maintain identical starting alloy composition and similar processing steps aside from the modified atmosphere and cooling rate.
measurements: XRD phase analysis to quantify amorphous fraction.
DSC/TGA to measure onset of crystallization and supercooled liquid region.
Critical sample thickness for fully amorphous microstructure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no consistent increase (≥20%) in the maximum fully amorphous sample thickness or no measurable delay in crystallization for the high-purity/high-rate condition compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The cooling rates were systematically varied, with slow cooling averaging approximately 52 K/s, accelerated cooling at 3018 K/s, and melt-spinning achieving rapid cooling rates in the range of 10⁵–10⁶ K/s. The intensity profile of the diffraction rings observed in TEM, with two broad peaks at wave vector values of k = 1.169 nm−1 and k = 2.002 nm−1, corresponds to characteristic features of reciprocal space scattering in amorphous structures. These values are indicative of the short-range atomic ordering typical of metallic glasses based on transition metals and phosphorus. Cooling rates significantly influence the microstructure and phase composition of the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy. Slow cooling after arc melting results in a complex microstructure comprising multiple crystalline phases such as FCC “A”, tetragonal “B”, “C”, “D”, and orthorhombic “E”, while faster cooling after a short electric arc pulse reduces the number of phases to primarily FCC “A” and tetragonal “D”. Very rapid cooling using the melt-spinning method results in an amorphous structure, as confirmed by XRD and TEM analyses. Phosphorus addition enhances the alloy’s glass-forming ability during rapid cooling. The amorphous structure observed in the melt-spun ribbon demonstrates that the combination of phosphorus and high mixing entropy promotes the formation of amorphous phases during extremely fast cooling. However, further studies are necessary to understand the influence of phosphorus on mechanical properties and limitations, such as reduced ductility. decision.trend: Recent studies on high-entropy and compositionally complex metallic glasses have shown that increasing total mixing entropy and controlling short-range order can both enhance glass stability. Earlier works demonstrated that high-entropy compositions enable unusual glass-to-glass transitions, and machine-learning models help identify factors improving glass-forming ability (GFA). In phosphorus-bearing alloys specifically, high cooling rates (e.g., melt-spinning) have successfully suppressed crystallization, resulting in enhanced amorphous fraction and delayed onset of transformations during heating. Nonetheless, it remains challenging to systematically identify a single processing strategy that yields robust, predictable improvements in both GFA and thermal stability for compositions that include phosphorus.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress in understanding the role of high configurational entropy and rapid quenching, a unified approach for reliably suppressing early nucleation and stabilizing amorphous phases in phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys remains elusive. The field lacks consensus on which singular, widely applicable processing measure most effectively targets both improved glass-forming ability and elevated thermal stability across a broad range of P-bearing alloys.
decision.lever: Refine the melt-spinning process under a high-purity inert atmosphere with a minimum cooling rate of 10^5 K/s, ensuring minimal oxygen ingress and rapid undercooling of the molten alloy prior to solidification.
decision.why: By combining high-purity conditions with sufficiently fast quenching, the number of potent heterogeneous nucleation sites that accelerate crystallization is minimized, improving glass-forming ability and delaying the onset of devitrification. Prior work on Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 showed that rapid cooling greatly increases the amorphous fraction and thermal stability; these observations guide the hypothesis that controlling input gas purity and elevating cooling rates markedly extend the supercooled liquid region and reduce nuclei formation. We predict that, relative to a baseline process with lower cooling rates or less controlled melt conditions, the new approach will yield at least a 20% increase in critical sample thickness and raise the onset temperature for crystallization. The method may be less effective if oxygen contamination cannot be sufficiently minimized or if the cooling rate is below the critical threshold for the specific alloy composition. A suitable falsification experiment would be to cast parallel samples under both standard and enhanced (high-purity + >10^5 K/s) melt-spinning conditions and measure their amorphous fraction and crystallization onset temperature. Failure to observe any consistent increase in these metrics would invalidate the hypothesis.
